strengths: The core idea (Value Sign Flip) is simple, intuitive, and computationally elegant: it requires only a single forward pass (vs. two for CFG) and integrates naturally into attention computation for both MMDiT-style and cross-attention architectures, addressing a real efficiency gap since CFG is largely incompatible with distilled few-step models.

The paper provides fairly thorough engineering analysis of implementation details needed to make the idea work correctly (attention masking/duplication of negative tokens, attention bias term, padding removal), each justified with ablations and visualizations (Figs. 4-6, 9).

Broad experimental scope: comparisons against NASA, NAG (and a re-tuned NAG++), non-few-step CFG, and several external baselines (GPT-4o, Janus-4o, Qwen-Image, Generate+Edit pipeline), plus trade-off curves (positive/quality vs. negative score) that give a more complete picture than single-point comparisons.

Demonstrates cross-architecture applicability (SD3.5 MMDiT and Wan 2.1 + CausVid video model with cross-attention), and reports runtime/VRAM costs showing the method is competitive with or cheaper than baselines.

Reasonably candid discussion of limitations, including failure on Flux Schnell, MLLM quality-score miscalibration (Fig. 6), and qualitative cases where VSF over-removes content or underperforms NAG/NASA.
weaknesses: Quantitative evaluation depends entirely on a single MLLM judge (LLaMA-4 Maverick) for both positive/negative adherence and quality scoring; the paper itself shows this judge is unreliable for quality (Fig. 6, heavily distorted images scored 70-90), which undermines confidence in the main quantitative claims. A promised human evaluation for pairwise comparison is mentioned but its results/details are not actually reported in the manuscript.

The benchmark dataset (200 prompts) is self-generated via ChatGPT o3 specifically for this paper and evaluation questions are also machine-generated; there is no comparison to established negation/negative-prompt benchmarks (e.g., NegBench-style datasets referenced in related work), raising concerns about circularity and generalizability of the reported gains.

Qualitative results (Fig. 7, Appendix) show VSF frequently over-removes content unrelated to the negative prompt (e.g., keyboard, windshield, tomato shape distortion) or fails on abstract/sub-concept negations (e.g., "dog" from "pet", "male" from "scientist"), suggesting the method's advantage over NAG/NASA is inconsistent and sometimes reversed.

NASA was reimplemented from scratch because official code was unavailable, introducing a risk that the baseline comparison is not fully faithful to the original method, and no validation against reported NASA numbers is provided.

The method fails outright on Flux Schnell's two-stream/one-stream attention architecture, and this negative result is only briefly mentioned without deeper analysis, limiting confidence in the claimed general applicability to "any transformer-based diffusion or flow-matching model."

Statistical testing is limited to McNemar's test for the negative score only; no significance testing is reported for positive-prompt adherence or quality score comparisons, despite these being central to the trade-off narrative.

Presentation quality has multiple typos/grammatical issues (e.g., "Tunning", "Comparsion", "computatio nal", inconsistent capitalization) and some notation/equation explanations (e.g., Eq. 6) are dense and could be clarified further for reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: negative-prompt guidance is broken in few-step/distilled diffusion and flow-matching models where CFG is either incompatible or produces severe over-saturation artifacts.

The proposed Value Sign Flip mechanism is conceptually simple, has small computational overhead compared to a full extra CFG pass, and is shown to work across both cross-attention (Wan/CausVid) and MMDiT-style (SD3.5) architectures with the needed masking/duplication tricks worked out in detail.

Fairly extensive empirical effort: ablations on masking, duplication, attention bias, padding removal, an alternative 'Whole Embedding Flip' baseline, a hyperparameter trade-off sweep (positive/negative/quality curves) against NAG and NASA, and comparisons with several external systems (GPT-4o, Janus-4o, Qwen-Image, a generate-then-edit pipeline).

The paper is reasonably candid about limitations: it reports that the method fails to improve results on Flux Schnell, shows qualitative failure cases (e.g., laptop keyboard, statue nose), and explicitly discusses known unreliability of the MLLM quality judge (Figure 6).
weaknesses: The entire quantitative evaluation pipeline rests on a single MLLM-as-judge (Llama-4-Maverick) for both prompt-adherence and quality scores; the authors themselves show this judge assigns high 'quality' scores (70-100) to clearly distorted images, which directly undermines the validity of the main results in Table 2 and the trade-off curves in Figures 8-9. No large-scale human evaluation is reported in the main results to corroborate these numbers (a human study is mentioned only in passing, without details or results shown).

In the external baseline comparison (Table 1), GPT-4o achieves a substantially higher negative-prompt score (0.705) than VSF (0.545), so the paper's own headline claim of superior negative-prompt adherence does not hold against the strongest baseline; VSF is only 'second-best' by the authors' own account, which weakens the central contribution.

Baseline tuning appears uneven and potentially biased: NAG hyperparameters were manually re-tuned by the authors into a 'NAG++' variant 'pushed to the edge of acceptable visual quality' without a systematic sweep ('not swept to avoid overfitting'), while VSF's own trade-off curves are drawn from a dedicated hyperparameter sweep — this asymmetry makes the head-to-head comparisons less trustworthy.

Method generality is limited: it fails to meaningfully improve negative-prompt adherence on Flux Schnell (a widely used few-step model with a different one-/two-stream attention design), and the paper offers no clear diagnosis or fix, just defers this to future work, which questions the claimed broad applicability to 'MMDiT-style architectures' in general.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to NASA/NAG: the core idea (subtract/flip negative value contributions weighted by attention strength) is a natural extension of existing negative-guidance-in-attention-space methods (NASA, NAG, Koulischer et al.), and the paper's main technical additions are largely implementation-level (masking, duplication, bias, padding removal) rather than a fundamentally new formulation.

Reproducibility concerns: the evaluation dataset (200 GPT-o3-generated prompt pairs) is not clearly released, no code/checkpoints availability is mentioned, and the qualitative Wan/Flux examples are described as 'not meant to reflect comprehensive performance,' limiting confidence in replicability of the claimed gains.

Several reported outcomes are mixed or contradict the paper's stronger claims: NAG achieves a higher quality score than VSF in Table 2, VSF sometimes removes more content than intended (e.g., laptop keyboard, car windshield) or underperforms on entire categories (leaves example), and the appendix qualitative study on Wan concludes 'the outputs of VSF and NAG are comparable' rather than VSF being clearly superior, which is inconsistent with the abstract's claim of 'significantly improves negative prompt adherence...even than CFG.'

Presentation issues: notation and terminology are occasionally imprecise or inconsistently used (e.g., 'quality score' semantics change between sections, statistical significance testing via McNemar is only briefly mentioned for negative scores without full reporting), and some claims (e.g., 'we found removing it has no effects at all' regarding padding) are asserted without supporting quantitative evidence.

strengths: Addresses a real and practical problem: CFG is largely broken/incompatible with few-step distilled diffusion models, and existing negative-guidance alternatives (NASA, NAG) use a fixed guidance strength that cannot adapt across layers/steps/regions.

The proposed Value Sign Flip (VSF) mechanism is simple and well-motivated, and the paper carefully works through the engineering details needed to make it work in MMDiT-style concatenated-sequence architectures (negative prompt duplication, attention masking to avoid unwanted P->N and N->N interactions, attention bias to offset the 'distraction' effect of including a negative prompt, and padding removal) — these ablations show the design choices are not arbitrary.

Reasonably thorough empirical study: comparisons against NASA, NAG (with re-tuned NAG++), CFG on a non-few-step model, and several external baselines (GPT-4o, Janus-4o, Qwen-Image, Generate+Edit pipeline), plus a Pareto-style trade-off analysis (positive/negative/quality score frontier) rather than single-point comparisons, which is a more rigorous way to compare guidance methods with different operating points.

Demonstrates generality beyond a single model: results are also shown on a video diffusion model (Wan 2.1 + CausVid LoRA), and a computational cost table shows the method is close to single-pass runtime/memory, addressing efficiency concerns directly.

The paper is reasonably self-critical: it explicitly discusses failure cases (e.g., Flux Schnell not benefiting, MLLM quality-score inflation on distorted images as shown in Figure 6, ambiguity in negative prompts affecting scores), and includes an ablation comparing to a simpler 'Whole Embedding Flip' baseline to justify the more complex design.
Provides some mechanistic insight via attention-map visualizations showing the negative attention concentrating on regions corresponding to the undesired concept.
weaknesses: The primary quantitative evaluation relies on an MLLM-as-judge (Llama-4-Maverick) for both prompt adherence and image quality; the paper itself acknowledges this judge is unreliable (e.g., Figure 6 shows a severely distorted image rated 70/100) and admits 'the mistakes are minor' without rigorous quantification of judge error rate.

A promised human evaluation ('we also did a human evaluation between our model and NAG for pairwise comparison') is mentioned but no results, numbers, agreement statistics, or methodology for this human study are reported anywhere in the paper, which weakens confidence in the main quantitative claims.

The evaluation dataset (200 LLM-generated prompt pairs, 2 seeds) is custom-built via ChatGPT o3 rather than an established benchmark, which limits reproducibility, comparability to future work, and could be biased by the same generation process used to create evaluation questions.

Generalization is limited: the method fails to meaningfully help on Flux Schnell (a different one-stream/two-stream DiT architecture), which somewhat undercuts the claimed general applicability to 'any transformer-based diffusion or flow-matching model'; the reasons for this failure are only briefly speculated about, not analyzed.

The core technical novelty is incremental relative to NASA/NAG — the central idea (adaptive per-token guidance strength via a sign-flipped value in attention) is a relatively small conceptual step beyond existing attention-space negative guidance methods, and much of the paper's contribution is in engineering details for MMDiT compatibility rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Statistical testing (McNemar's test) is reported only for the negative score, not consistently for positive/quality scores, and the trade-off curves are built from 'critical points' with limited discussion of variance across seeds/prompts.

Some acknowledged qualitative failure modes (e.g., unnatural physical formations, removing more than intended, worse performance on abstract sub-concept negation such as 'male' or 'dog') suggest the method's robustness is still limited on harder cases, and these are not deeply analyzed beyond anecdote.
The paper has minor clarity/writing issues (e.g., 'Padding Removel' header, some awkward phrasing) suggesting incomplete polishing, and no explicit statement on code/data release for reproducibility.

strengths: Proposes a simple, theoretically grounded method (Value Sign Flip) for negative prompt guidance in few-step diffusion/flow models, with a formal proof that it is equivalent to token-weighted subtraction using attention-map-derived weights.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple architectures (SD3.5-Large-Turbo, Flux Schnell, Wan 2.1 video model) and against multiple baselines (NASA, NAG, CFG, generate-then-edit pipelines, GPT-4o, Nano Banana, Qwen-Image, Janus-4o), showing consistently favorable trade-offs between positive/negative prompt adherence and image quality.
Careful ablation studies (whole-embedding-flip variant, masking/bias/duplication components, hyperparameter sweeps producing trade-off curves) that support the design choices in the method.

Introduces a new challenging benchmark (NegGenBench) targeting hard negative prompts (implicit removal of essential object parts) and fine-tunes a negation-aware MLLM (NegAwareQwen) to improve automatic evaluation, with human validation used to check the automatic metrics.
Efficiency analysis shows the method avoids the two-pass cost of CFG and has runtime/memory close to a single forward pass, which is practically relevant for few-step/real-time generation.

Includes interesting extended use cases (style avoidance, abstract/anti-aesthetic image generation) and thorough appendix material (attention map visualizations, failure case analysis, adaptation to other DiT models) that add depth to the evaluation.

Reasonably transparent about limitations (failure cases with strongly associated concepts, MLLM evaluation noise, need for masking due to lack of efficient attention kernel support) and commits to releasing code/dataset/models.
weaknesses: The core automatic evaluation relies heavily on LLaMA-4-Maverick and a self-trained NegAwareQwen judge rather than established, widely validated metrics; human validation is based on only 10 prompts with 2 seeds (20 images) per method, which is a very small sample to confidently establish reliability of the automatic scores used for the main claims.

Main results tables report single numbers without variance/error bars despite using only 1-2 seeds in several experiments, making it hard to assess statistical significance of reported differences (e.g., VSF vs. NAG negative scores).
Baseline hyperparameter tuning (e.g., NAG Strong) is done by the authors themselves post hoc, which raises some concern about comparison fairness, even though this is partially acknowledged.

The proposed benchmark (NegGenBench) is entirely constructed by the authors using an LLM (ChatGPT o3) without external validation of prompt diversity/difficulty or independent human curation, limiting confidence in its generality as a benchmark contribution.

The method still requires nontrivial architecture-specific engineering (attention masking, negative-prompt duplication, bias term) for MMDiT-style models, and the authors note real-world runtime exceeds the theoretical minimum due to lack of efficient masked-attention kernels, partially offsetting the claimed efficiency benefit.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to NASA and NAG, essentially adding token/attention-map-based dynamic weighting to NASA's framework, an extension direction that was already suggested as future work in the NAG paper.

Failure cases (e.g., house without roof, cat without whiskers) show the method can still fail when the negative concept is strongly entangled with the positive concept, and no quantitative failure-rate analysis is provided to characterize how often this occurs across the benchmark.
